How near-duplicate leakage inflates reported accuracy in high-entropy-alloy phase prediction

A reproducible audit of 1103 experimentally reported alloys, and the true ceiling of the classical phase-formation criteria
Fengrui (AI-assisted computational analysis) · generated 2026-09-11 11:46 Beijing time · data: Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.6403257 (CC-BY-4.0)

Abstract

Background. Machine-learning phase prediction for high-entropy alloys (HEAs) routinely reports 85–95% accuracy. Almost all of these numbers come from randomly split train/test sets, yet experimental alloy data are highly redundant in composition space: within one chemical system (same set of elements) there are many near-duplicate samples that differ only in stoichiometry.

Methods. On a public set of 1103 experimentally reported HEAs (350 solid-solution, 753 non-solid-solution) I ran four independent experiments: (i) an audit of the redundancy structure; (ii) an evaluation of the classical phase-formation criteria (δ, ΔHmix, Ω, VEC, Δχ and their conjunctions); (iii) a comparison of identical models under random-stratified versus chemical-system-grouped cross-validation; (iv) a controlled, size-matched, test-set-paired experiment plus a nearest-neighbour composition-distance analysis.

Results. The 1103 alloys correspond to only 449 distinct element sets; 74.9% of alloys share their chemical system with at least one other alloy; the largest single system holds 45 alloys; 59 compositions are exact duplicates. The best classical rule (δ + ΔHmix + Ω conjunction) reaches balanced accuracy 0.753 (95% CI 0.725–0.779), comparable to the best single descriptor after cross-validated threshold tuning (Ω, 0.742). In the controlled paired experiment, a gradient-boosted model scores +0.133 balanced accuracy higher under a random split than under a chemical-system-disjoint split (95% CI [0.063, 0.196], Wilcoxon p = 2.0e-03), whereas logistic regression gains only +0.023. Under the random split, 25.5% of test alloys have a training neighbour at L1 composition distance < 0.05, versus 2.8% under the disjoint split. Under the hardest extrapolation setting (leave-one-element-out) mean balanced accuracy falls to 0.665.

Conclusions. On this dataset the random-split inflation is roughly 0.12–0.15 balanced accuracy for high-capacity models and 0.02–0.05 for strongly regularised linear models. The inflation is driven by near-duplicate samples in the training set, not by the use of composition features. HEA machine-learning studies should report at least one chemical-system-disjoint split and treat leave-one-element extrapolation as a standard stress test.

1. Research question

The standard pipeline in the HEA phase-prediction literature is: aggregate a few hundred to a few thousand "composition → phase" records from the literature, compute empirical descriptors, train a classifier, and report accuracy on a randomly split test set. Reported accuracies typically fall in the 0.85–0.95 range.

The problem is that experimental HEA data are not independent and identically distributed. For AlCoCrFeNi, for instance, the literature contains dozens of variants that differ only in Al or Cr fraction. They share an identical element set, their composition vectors are extremely close, and their phase labels are usually identical. Under a random split these near-duplicates land in both the training and the test set, so a model can score well simply by memorising the label of that chemical system rather than learning transferable physics.

This work addresses three quantifiable questions:

  1. Q1 — How severe is the near-duplicate structure in this widely used public dataset?
  2. Q2 — How much accuracy disappears once that convenience is removed, and does the loss depend on model capacity?
  3. Q3 — What is the true discriminative power of the classical phase-formation criteria, and are they already close to the ceiling imposed by univariate information?

I do not claim that leakage itself is a new discovery — it is systematically discussed in machine learning and cheminformatics (e.g. DataSAIL, Nature Communications 2025). The contribution here is a reproducible, size-matched, statistically tested quantification on one specific, repeatedly used HEA dataset, together with a directly reusable splitting protocol.

2. Data

Public dataset Materials for Design Open Repository. High Entropy Alloys (Zenodo record 6403257, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.6403257, licence CC-BY-4.0). The raw file 2022-03-31-HEAs_dataset_v2.xlsx is never modified; the whole pipeline reads it only.

1103labelled alloys
350 / 753solid solution / not

2.1 Labels and features

The primary label is the four-class S_Phase field (SS solid solution / SS+IM solid solution plus intermetallic / IM intermetallic / AM amorphous). After dropping 14 unlabelled records, 1103 alloys remain. The main task is binarised to SS versus non-SS (350 positives, base rate 0.317).

Features come in two blocks:

  • Composition: 78 elemental mole fractions (normalised from the raw atomic ratios; row sums are exactly 1).
  • Descriptors: 9 empirical quantities — atomic size mismatch δ, mixing enthalpy ΔHmix, ideal mixing entropy Sid, Ω = TmΔSmix/|ΔHmix| (recomputed here from the Yang & Zhang definition), valence electron concentration VEC, σVEC, electronegativity difference Δχ, mean electronegativity χ, and melting temperature Tm.

Note: Ω is missing for 1.16% of rows (it diverges as ΔHmix → 0); linear models use median imputation while tree models handle missing values natively.

2.2 Redundancy structure (answers Q1)

The 1103 alloys correspond to only 449 distinct element sets; 74.9% (826 alloys) sit in a system shared with at least one other alloy, and the largest single system contains 45 alloys. A further 59 alloys have compositions that are exact duplicates at four-decimal precision. Consequently, under a random split the overwhelming majority of test samples have a same-system near-relative in the training set.

3. Methods

3.1 Models

Two deliberately chosen model families, to separate capacity effects from leakage effects:

  • logreg — median imputation + standardisation + logistic regression (C = 1.0, class_weight='balanced'): strongly regularised, low capacity.
  • hgb — histogram gradient-boosted trees (150 iterations, learning rate 0.08, 15 leaves): high capacity, able to memorise local patterns.

3.2 Four evaluation protocols

  1. Random stratified split (the literature default): StratifiedKFold(5), 3 repeats.
  2. Chemical-system-grouped split: StratifiedGroupKFold(5) with the element set as the group, 3 repeats — no chemical system crosses the train/test boundary.
  3. Controlled paired experiment (primary evidence): a fixed 20% stratified test set T, and three training sets:
    · TrainA_all — every non-test alloy (882 alloys);
    · TrainA_matched — TrainA randomly subsampled to the size of TrainB (446 alloys), 3 repeats;
    · TrainB_disjoint — non-test alloys after removing every alloy that shares an element set with any alloy in T (446 alloys).
    The test set is identical and the training sets are the same size, so the only difference is the presence of near-duplicate samples. Repeated over 10 independent test splits and compared with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
    Note: TrainB retains on average only 50.6% of TrainA's rows; without size matching, the accuracy drop would be confounded with simply having less data.
  4. Leave-one-element-out: for each of the 18 elements occurring in ≥45 alloys, train with no alloy containing element X and test only on alloys that do contain X — the hardest extrapolation setting.

3.3 Statistics and reproducibility

Metrics are balanced accuracy (more meaningful than plain accuracy under class imbalance), MCC and ROC-AUC. 95% confidence intervals for binary metrics come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples; paired comparisons use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. All random seeds are fixed, the raw data are read-only, and every number in this report is written by the build script directly from the result files rather than transcribed by hand.

4. Results

4.1 What the classical criteria are really worth (answers Q3)

If the criteria worked, points of the same class would cluster inside the window. Figure 2 shows extensive overlap: the solid-solution window is equally crowded with intermetallic and amorphous samples.

Key observations:

  • The best classical rule is the δ + ΔHmix + Ω conjunction, at 0.753 — better than the majority-class baseline (0.500) but far from reliable; its MCC is only 0.474.
  • Plain accuracy is misleading here: the majority-class baseline achieves 0.683, higher than the δ criterion alone at 0.663, because positives are only 31.7% of the data. Reporting "accuracy" on this task therefore carries almost no information.
  • The classical rules systematically over-predict solid solution: the three-rule conjunction has sensitivity 0.786 and specificity 0.720. Adding the VEC constraint lifts specificity to 0.788 but collapses sensitivity to 0.569.

To test whether the criteria merely have badly chosen thresholds, I ran a 5-fold cross-validated threshold search for each descriptor (thresholds selected on the training fold only):

The exception: the VEC rule separates lattices almost perfectly

On the pure-FCC and pure-BCC alloys (220 alloys), the VEC rule (VEC ≥ 8 → FCC, VEC ≤ 6.87 → BCC) is 100% accurate on the 163 decidable cases (coverage 74.1%), with 57 alloys falling in the ambiguity window. Median VEC is 8.12 for FCC and 4.91 for BCC. This shows that "can a solid solution form" and "which lattice forms" are two problems of completely different difficulty: the latter is governed by electron concentration, whereas the former is strongly influenced by kinetics and non-equilibrium processing.

4.2 Where the classical criteria fail

Taking the four-rule conjunction as an example, 160 alloys are falsely predicted as solid solution and 151 true solid solutions are missed.

  • False positives concentrate in SS+IM (104 alloys): the criterion says "a solid solution can form", but experiment observes solid solution coexisting with an intermetallic. This is an inherent limitation of a thermodynamic window criterion — it tests possibility, not uniqueness.
  • False negatives concentrate in refractory HEAs: the Mo+Nb+Ti+V+Zr system accounts for 17 missed cases, the most of any system. The classical windows were fitted mainly on 3d transition-metal systems and transfer poorly to refractory chemistries.

(2) The controlled paired experiment: isolating leakage

The comparison above has one flaw — the grouped split trains on less data. The controlled experiment removes that confound by matching training-set size.

Headline number. With a fixed test set and matched training-set size, merely having near-duplicate alloys of the same chemical system in the training set gives the gradient-boosted model +0.133 balanced accuracy (95% CI [0.063, 0.196]); logistic regression differs by only +0.023, with a confidence interval that includes zero. The inflation reported in the literature is therefore governed by model capacity: the more flexible the model, the more it can memorise local samples.

Notably, giving the model only the 9 descriptors — no composition at all — still inflates the boosted trees by +0.116. The root cause is not "using composition features" but the presence of samples in the training set that are nearly identical to the test samples, which any sufficiently flexible model can exploit.

The mechanism is plain: under a random split, a quarter of all test alloys have an almost identical counterpart in the training set (L1 distance below 0.05); under a chemical-system-disjoint split that share drops to 2.8%. The high scores on those test samples reflect memory, not generalisation.

4.5 The hardest extrapolation: leave-one-element-out

Averaged over 18 elements, balanced accuracy is 0.665 (sd 0.133, range 0.420–0.931), with mean ROC-AUC 0.776. Against the random-split figure of 0.859, that is a gap of nearly 0.2 balanced accuracy.

The claim "a model can predict HEA phases" is only meaningful when the extrapolation condition is stated.

5. Discussion

5.1 Direct implications for HEA machine-learning practice

  • Random-split numbers should not be read as generalisation ability. On this dataset high-capacity models are inflated by roughly 0.12–0.15 balanced accuracy. Where the literature reports 0.90+ using random splits and tree ensembles, a substantial part of that may come from near-duplicate memorisation.
  • Report at least one chemical-system-disjoint split. The implementation cost is one line (GroupKFold with the element set as the group), but the effect on the honesty of the conclusion is large. This is the most practical recommendation of this work.
  • Report balanced accuracy and MCC, not accuracy. The SS base rate here is only 31.7%, so predicting "not SS" everywhere already yields 0.683 accuracy.
  • Use leave-one-element extrapolation as a stress test. It answers the question materials discovery actually cares about: does this still work in a chemical system the model has never seen?
  • Separate the two tasks. Lattice type (FCC/BCC, where the VEC rule reaches 100% accuracy) is far easier than "can a solid solution form". Merging them into a single "phase prediction" label hides the real difficulty difference.

5.2 Relation to prior work

Data leakage is a mature topic in machine learning, and cheminformatics already has dedicated splitting tools (e.g. DataSAIL, 2025) and reviews; there is also discussion of random splits overestimating performance in materials informatics. This work does not claim to discover the phenomenon. It contributes a size-matched, controlled paired measurement of the magnitude on one specific, repeatedly used HEA dataset, a mechanistic explanation via nearest-neighbour distance, and evidence that the magnitude is strongly tied to model capacity.

5.3 Transferable methodology

The design — "fixed test set + group-wise exclusion + size-matched subsampling + paired test" — is not specific to HEAs. It applies to any data with a "one system, many stoichiometries" structure (catalysts, perovskites, battery electrolytes). Its value is turning leakage from a qualitative worry into a measurable quantity.

6. Limitations

  • Single data source. Conclusions rest on this one dataset. Redundancy levels differ across sources and cleaning conventions, so the inflation magnitude cannot be extrapolated to all HEA literature.
  • Label noise in the dataset itself. Records are aggregated from the literature with inconsistent processing routes (casting / sputtering / annealing), characterisation methods and phase criteria; the 196 "SS+IM" records are inherently intermediate. Some apparent "generalisation failures" are in fact definitional ambiguity.
  • The element set is an approximate grouping. Within one element set compositions can still differ widely; a stricter grouping (element set plus composition range) would yield a larger inflation, so the numbers here should be read as a lower bound.
  • Only two model families. The capacity–inflation relationship is consistent across both, but the capacity spectrum was not systematically swept.
  • Descriptor conventions. δ, ΔHmix, VEC and the others are taken from the dataset; Ω was recomputed here from the standard definition, so Ω-related conclusions would shift if the original definition differed slightly.
  • No hyper-parameter tuning. Models use fixed hyper-parameters to keep protocols comparable. Tuning would amplify capacity effects but would not change the direction of the conclusions.

7. Reproducibility

All code, intermediate results and figures live under research/; the raw data file is never modified.

research/
├── data/
│   ├── heas_v2.xlsx              # raw data (Zenodo 6403257, read-only)
│   ├── hea_processed.parquet     # cleaned analysis table
│   └── hea_processed.csv
├── code/
│   ├── hea_common.py             # loading / feature / grouping utilities
